pending.title: Israeli parliament erupts in chaos as Netanyahu bloc loses vote
pending.summary: Israel's deeply divided parliament descended into chaos on Wednesday as lawmakers traded insults, hurled accusations and shouted over one another, exposing bitter political divisions after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu 's far-right bloc suffered its first defeat in the newly elected Knesset. The confrontation erupted during the inaugural meeting of the Arrangements Committee, where extreme-right lawmaker Tally Gotliv was forcibly removed from proceedings after repeatedly interrupting fellow legislators, according to Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth . Committee chairman Roy Folkman, from former army chief Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party, ordered Gotliv, a member of National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's extremist Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party, to leave as tensions escalated. Gotliv continued shouting and protesting as she was escorted from the room, while Palestinian lawmakers chanted "Out, out", according to the Israeli newspaper. The disorder followed a significant political setback for Netanyahu, whose bloc lost a parliamentary vote on the committee's composition by 63 votes to 50. The proposal, backed by Eisenkot's bloc and Palestinian lawmakers, marked the first defeat for Netanyahu's allies since the October 27 Israeli elections, which left the prime minister, who is now serving in a caretaker capacity, without a parliamentary majority. Insults and bitter exchanges The committee meeting quickly deteriorated into a shouting match as lawmakers exchanged personal insults and accusations. Newly elected Likud lawmaker Erez Tadmor was branded a "weapons thief" by female legislators, referring to his previous conviction for stealing military equipment during his army service. Tadmor, who was sentenced to 45 days in prison over the offence, responded by calling lawmaker Merav Ben-Ari a "hen", triggering accusations of misogyny. He then attacked Eisenkot's bloc for cooperating with Palestinian parties, repeating accusations that they supported terrorism. "This is my second day in the Knesset and I am shocked," Tadmor said, according to Yedioth Ahronoth , before accusing rival lawmakers of rejecting Netanyahu's calls for unity. Tadmor also called Democrats lawmaker Naama Lazimi a "roadblocker", prompting her to respond sarcastically: "There is your unity." This was apparently a reference to Netanyahu's calls for a "national unity" government excluding Arab parties following the election. The confrontation escalated when Gotliv repeatedly interrupted Lazimi as she criticised the treatment of lawmakers and families of Israelis killed or taken captive during the war. Gotliv accused Lazimi of mocking Netanyahu's appearance, prompting another heated exchange before Folkman ordered her removal. Despite the chaotic proceedings, the committee approved the appointment of Yisrael Beiteinu leader Avigdor Lieberman to chair the temporary Foreign Affairs and Defence Committee. Liran Avisar Ben-Horin was also appointed to lead the temporary Finance Committee. Netanyahu attacks Palestinian lawmakers The clashes highlighted the growing divisions in Israeli politics as Netanyahu struggles to retain power following an election that denied his far-right bloc a governing majority. Palestinian parties have emerged as important players in the parliamentary arithmetic, with their support helping Eisenkot's bloc secure its first victory. Netanyahu has repeatedly attacked Palestinian lawmakers while simultaneously calling for a national unity government under his leadership. During a speech on Tuesday, he accused Palestinian parties of supporting "terrorism" and condemned Eisenkot's bloc for negotiating with them. His remarks prompted Eisenkot's Yashar party to cancel planned coalition talks with Likud, accusing Netanyahu of delivering a divisive speech. On Wednesday, Netanyahu renewed his appeal for unity, declaring that Israelis must come together in the face of security challenges. Extremist Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich echoed the appeal but warned against forming a government reliant on Palestinian parties, urging Eisenkot to reach an agreement with Netanyahu instead. Meanwhile, Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported that Netanyahu was attempting to prevent the newly formed Foreign Affairs and Defence Committee from convening in the coming days. The committee is responsible for parliamentary oversight of Israel's military and intelligence agencies, including the authority to question senior security officials. The political turmoil comes ahead of a November 17 vote to replace Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally, in another test of his bloc's dwindling parliamentary influence. Eisenkot is continuing negotiations to form a government, with the latest confrontations underscoring the hostility between rival Israeli factions and the central role Palestinian lawmakers could play in determining Netanyahu's political future.

pending.title: Houthis deny targeting Mecca amid Saudi missile interceptions
pending.summary: Yemen's Houthi movement has denied targeting Mecca after Saudi Arabia said it intercepted drones heading towards Islam's holiest city, while debris from two ballistic missiles fell in parts of the surrounding province. The Saudi-led military coalition said on Wednesday that its air defences had destroyed three cruise missiles headed towards Riyadh and two drones launched towards the Mecca and southern regions of Saudi Arabia. It also reported intercepting two missiles directed towards the west of the kingdom. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree rejected the allegation that the group had attempted to strike Mecca, describing the Saudi account as false and insisting that Houthi operations were directed at oil infrastructure and military installations. Saree said the group had instead launched a drone attack against an oil pumping station in Yanbu, on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast, and fired three cruise missiles at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. Saudi authorities did not confirm an attack on the Yanbu facility. The competing claims about the intended targets could not be independently verified. Early on Thursday, Saudi civil defence reported a separate incident involving two ballistic missiles it said had been launched towards the Mecca region and intercepted by Saudi air defences. Saudi state television identified two places where debris fell: Sabuhah village, approximately 35 kilometres northeast of the Grand Mosque, and Wadi al-Maghmas, about 21 kilometres east of the mosque. Saudi civil defence called the alleged targeting of civilian sites a violation of international humanitarian law. The Houthis had not issued a specific response to the latest report of falling missile debris by early Thursday, although they have repeatedly denied targeting either Mecca or Medina, the two holiest cities in Islam. Mecca is home to the Kaaba and the Grand Mosque and is the destination of the annual Hajj pilgrimage. Allegations that it has been deliberately targeted have particular religious and political sensitivity across the Muslim world. Renewed fighting across Yemen The latest Saudi-Houthi war of words comes amid intense fighting in Yemen following the September breakdown of the truce that had largely frozen the conflict since 2022. The Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, say their missile and drone strikes against Saudi Arabia are retaliation for Saudi attacks on areas under their control. Riyadh has intensified air strikes against Houthi positions, while the group has attacked or claimed attacks against airports, oil facilities and military installations. Saudi air defences also reported intercepting missiles aimed at Riyadh on Tuesday. An attack on King Khalid International Airport last month killed 13 people and injured more than 300, according to Reuters . On Sunday, an attack attributed to the Houthis damaged a Saudi Aramco administrative building in Riyadh. Fighting has also continued inside Yemen. Forces loyal to the internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, claimed on Wednesday to have killed or wounded 138 Houthi fighters in attacks across several provinces, while the Houthis said they had struck a Saudi-backed military command facility in Aden's al-Buraiqa district. Neither side's battlefield claims could be independently verified. The human cost is rising. The World Health Organisation said fighting had killed 2,098 people and wounded 9,657 as of 8 November, while more than 320,000 people had been displaced since the beginning of August. The renewed fighting has also raised concerns over shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the strategic passage connecting the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.

The capability was on display at the Royal Navy’s recent commissioning of its first Autonomous Squadron, featured as part of the service’s developing Hybrid Fleet. This new capability is designed to provide persistent surveillance and early warning against emerging aerial threats in maritime environments, helping to protect naval assets, commercial shipping, ports, and critical national infrastructure. Operating independently or alongside conventional naval vessels, the system offers the potential to extend surveillance coverage, provide early warning of airborne threats and support force protection missions across a range of operational environments. The award follows a successful programme of development and shore and sea-based trials conducted by Saab UK and Kraken, where the experimental system demonstrated its ability to detect, track and classify airborne targets while operating autonomously in challenging maritime conditions. Today’s contract award supports that vision and demonstrates how Saab helps our customers to embracing innovative autonomous technologies that strengthen national security. Together with Kraken, we have moved from concept to operational adoption at an exceptional speed. Project BEEHIVE has taken its first major step in integrating complex payloads. The K3 – Sea Giraffe 1X combination will allow us to deliver an air surveillance picture up threat allowing early detection of hostile air tracks for subsequent engagement” said Captain Adam Ballard, Royal Navy Deputy Commander Surface Flotilla. “K3 Scout was designed from the outset to integrate with mission-ready payloads. Our modular bay allows the Royal Navy to re-role the boat rapidly for surveillance, counter-drone or strike, without changing the underlying platform. Giraffe 1X adds proven counter-UAS radar to our range of payloads and is one of many we’re developing with our partners.” Said Mal Crease, CEO and Founder, Kraken Technology Group. pending.title: Israel to launch military strikes without opposition approval
pending.summary: Israeli caretaker Defence Minister Israel Katz said Thursday that the outgoing coalition does not need permission from the opposition to decide on fresh military operations, following calls to show restraint. "We do not need approval from the opposition or any legal authority" for the army to carry out strikes in any of the arenas where it operates, Katz wrote on X. His comments came as the Israeli military killed at least 10 people in Gaza in the deadliest strikes since Israel's election last month. The leader of the opposition bloc, Gadi Eisenkot , has called on caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to show restraint, warning that the use of force without a "direct and immediate threat" could have "disastrous consequences for Israeli democracy and for citizens' trust". Netanyahu repeatedly threatened to resume the Iran war on the campaign trail for elections last month, warning of threats and even posting an image of a nuclear bomb destroying Tel Aviv. Katz said Thursday that the outgoing coalition had "demonstrated resolve and sound judgement in dealing with Iran, in full coordination with the IDF -- and that will remain the case now, as circumstances require". Netanyahu agreed to meet Thursday with Eisenkot to discuss national security following the row over whether the outgoing government can resume the conflict. In a short joint statement, Eisenkot and Netanyahu said they would meet at the prime minister's office for a briefing attended by Netanyahu's military aide. The announcement came a day after Eisenkot, who has a mandate to try to form a new government, accused Netanyahu of refusing to brief him, in what he called a deviation from protocol. Avigdor Liberman, a key member of Eisenkot's political bloc who has been named head of a parliamentary committee on foreign and defence affairs, also criticised Netanyahu on Thursday. "I warn you: a caretaker government is not allowed to make decisions that could drag Israel into war without parliamentary oversight and without the full consent of all security agencies," said Liberman, a hawkish former aide to Netanyahu who has become a strident critic. Neither Liberman nor Eisenkot mentioned Iran directly. Netanyahu's office has hit back, saying Wednesday that Eisenkot, a former military chief, was politicising national security. Since last year Netanyahu has twice ordered major bombing campaigns against Iran in partnership with US President Donald Trump. Both leaders said afterwards that they had severely set back Iran's efforts to build nuclear weapons, which the clerical state denies pursuing. Trump has allied himself with Netanyahu but in recent days has said the focus is on diplomacy, after he also suffered a setback in elections, partly due to the war. Eisenkot has until 6 December to form a government, although President Isaac Herzog can give him an extension until 20 December. Both Eisenkot's broad left-to-right coalition and Netanyahu's bloc of hard-right and religious parties fell short of a majority in Israel's October polls. Eisenkot is exploring options to form a government, with Liberman demanding he not work with Israeli-Arab lawmakers, whose numbers soared in the elections on the back of anger over Netanyahu. pending.summary: Ireland: Watchdog accused of stalling probe into Microsoft hosting Israeli military app Submitted by Areeb Ullah on Thu, 11/12/2026 - 11:10 Data monitor criticised over complaints that Ireland's Microsoft data centres host a tool to track Palestinians A protest at a Microsoft data centre campus in West Dublin in November (EKO/Bryan Meade) Off Irish lawmakers are calling for an investigation into Ireland 's data regulator over concerns that Microsoft's data centre campus outside Dublin hosts an app used by Israel to control the movements of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza. Last year, rights groups EKO and the Irish Centre for Civil Liberties (ICCL) filed a complaint with Ireland’s Data Protection Commission (DPC), raising concerns that Microsoft’s Grange Castle data centre was hosting elements of the Almunasseq app , used by the Israeli army to monitor Palestinians. The DPC has still not given a definitive response to the rights groups over the status of the complaint. Sinead Gibney, who serves in the Dail Eireann, the Irish parliament's lower house, said Microsoft's Irish data centres are "fuelling the crime of apartheid against Palestinians" in the West Bank and Gaza. “Microsoft must be held accountable and I’ll be pushing for the Department of Enterprise to fully investigate this matter in light of the wealth of UN reports detailing the apartheid system," she told Middle East Eye. "I'm calling on Microsoft to explain why it’s providing the Israeli government with the tools and technologies to sustain its system of apartheid – a system under which millions of Palestinians are being denied basic human rights." The complaint was submitted on behalf of a Palestinian resident of Gaza and the West Bank, as well as a European Union citizen, based on evidence provided by a whistleblower. Evidence seen by MEE and gathered by EKO and the ICCL showed that Israel used Microsoft’s Azure cloud computing platform to host elements of the Almunasseq app. According to the complaint, Microsoft provides the “underlying” and “essential computer infrastructure” needed for the app to function, including cloud storage, database services and computing power. This means information collected from Palestinians using the app could be processed and stored on Microsoft’s infrastructure. Whistleblower evidence submitted with the complaint also showed that parts of the app are hosted in Microsoft’s data centres in Ireland, potentially bringing them within the scope of EU data protection laws. The evidence was submitted to the DPC, which did not respond to MEE’s request for comment. Microsoft also declined to comment. Surveillance and control Launched in 2020 by Cogat, the Israeli military body overseeing civilian affairs in the occupied Palestinian territories, Almunasseq, which means “the coordinator” in Arabic, allows the Israeli army to track users’ phone locations and access their notifications, downloaded or saved files, and their device’s camera. Previously, Palestinians seeking permits to enter Israel, generally for humanitarian reasons or family reunification, had to visit Cogat offices in person to have their status checked. Since the introduction of Almunasseq, however, they have been required to download the app to access permit-related services, including for work, education and healthcare, or to visit sick relatives in hospital. One respondent told EKO they stopped using the app after 2023, as movement restrictions in the occupied West Bank became increasingly severe. “The restrictions had become stricter, including requirements to confirm return through photographs and location sharing, among other measures,” the Palestinian said. “As a result, I deleted the application and disposed of the phone on which it had been installed, fearing that the occupation authorities might use it to monitor me and my private life. I subsequently purchased a new phone.” Beyond concerns over surveillance, multiple Palestinians told EKO that the app had been used to cancel thousands of permits issued to Palestinians in Gaza for medical treatment and work after October 2023. Children and elderly people were among those affected. According to EKO’s report, the app’s terms of use allow the Israeli military administration to block access or alter content at any time for “security or policy considerations”. pending.summary: Nadim Nashif, co-founder and CEO of the Arab Centre for Social Media Advancement ( 7amleh ), warns that the occupied Palestinian territories are becoming a testing ground for surveillance and AI technologies later exported to other countries. He argues that big tech companies are increasingly moving beyond providing digital services to supporting the technological infrastructure of military operations . In an interview with The New Arab after participating in the Trust Conference in London on 4 and 5 November, Nashif discussed information 7amleh had gathered from Meta employees, who said European governments, including the UK, had pressured the company to tighten restrictions on pro-Palestinian content, particularly after 7 October 2023. Unfortunately, there was no publicly available evidence establishing government intervention in specific cases. Nashif criticised Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, drawing on research published by 7amleh in June in collaboration with Fabio Cristiano, a researcher at Utrecht University in the Netherlands. The study examined 3,520 cases reported to the organisation's 7or ("Hurr") monitoring platform for digital violations between 2021 and 2025. One of its main findings, he says, was the repeated use of Meta's Dangerous Organisations and Individuals (DOI) policy to restrict Palestinian content. The policy is designed to target organisations and individuals classified as dangerous and covers cases involving terrorism and organised violence. "The company's perspective on Palestinians and pro-Palestinian content is a security-based one, as though this content is suspicious and must be dealt with through deletion or restrictions," Nashif said. Users received no adequate explanation of which policy they had allegedly violated in around 70 percent of documented cases, with Meta also failing to respond to almost half of the appeals 7amleh submitted. Meta's restrictions went beyond deleting posts and suspending accounts, and included reducing content reach, limiting its appearance in recommendations and restricting livestreaming—measures that users often find hard to detect or challenge. Regarding alleged European pressure, Nashif said Meta employees had spoken about government demands for stricter content moderation, justified on the grounds of combating antisemitism. He stressed that antisemitism is a form of racism that must be combatted, but said problems arise when such measures extend to legitimate expressions of solidarity with Palestinians or criticism of Israeli policies. In September, 7amleh published a report examining restrictions on pro-Palestinian content in six European countries, including Britain, which documented how the overlap between platform policies, national legislation and government pressure affected freedom of expression. Nashif believes the digital risks facing Palestinians extend well beyond the occupied territories. "What happens in Palestine does not stay in Palestine ," he said, pointing to the international spread of surveillance technologies developed or deployed in the Palestinian territories, and highlighting the role of former Israeli intelligence members in establishing tech companies that draw on their military experience. Pegasus spyware, developed by Israeli company NSO Group, was an example of surveillance technology which had spread beyond Israel into Arab countries. Nashif also warned of the additional risks posed by military use of AI, with IT systems now analysing enormous quantities of data and suggesting military targets, he said, citing the Lavender and Gospel systems, which which were investigated in connection with Israeli operations in Gaza. He adds that processing this volume of data requires massive amounts of energy and digital infrastructure, which necessitates holding IT companies providing cloud storage and AI services to militaries accountable for how their technologies are used. pending.title: Iranian men found guilty in UK of assisting Iranian intelligence
pending.summary: Two Iranian men were found guilty on Thursday of spying on dissident journalists in Britain on behalf of Iran's Revolutionary Guards, a case British police said reflected increasing activity by Iran. Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, was found guilty at Woolwich Crown Court of two offences and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, was convicted of one offence under ⁠Britain's National Security Act. Police said the convictions marked the first time Iranian nationals had been convicted under the National Security Act, introduced in 2023 to counter threats from foreign states including Iran, which the authorities say have risen sharply. Sepahvand was directed by the IRGC or "middlemen" for Iranian intelligence, Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans said, adding the case "highlights the continuing and increasing threat to the UK from Iran". Iran has repeatedly denied involvement in spying or any such activity, and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said he was "disturbed" by the arrests of Sepahvand and others in May 2025. Prosecutors said at the start of Sepahvand and Manesh's trial last month that they had been carrying out surveillance on journalists working for Iran International, a Persian-language television station which is critical of Iran's government, between August 2024 ​and March 2025. Sepahvand was convicted of assisting a foreign intelligence service and a second charge relating to what prosecutors said was a plan for Sepahvand to attack one or more of their targets. Manesh was convicted of assisting a foreign intelligence service, but acquitted of the second charge relating to preparing for an attack. They will both be sentenced next month. A third man, Shapoor ​Qalehali Khani Noori, 57, was acquitted of both charges.

But barbarity is not”: The Red Cross warns of a dangerous erosion of the rules of war War may be an enduring feature of human history, but its brutality is neither inevitable nor beyond restraint. That distinction lies at the heart of a stark warning from Mirjana Spoljaric, President of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), who argues that the international rules established to protect civilians are being progressively weakened amid proliferating armed conflicts, technological transformations and the retreat of diplomacy. “You may consider war a human condition,” Spoljaric tells France 24. “But brutality, barbarity, is not a human condition.” Her warning recalls the fundamental premise of the 1949 Geneva Conventions: even in war, there can be no lawless space, and certain red lines must never be crossed. Yet from Gaza and Ukraine to Sudan and Yemen, Spoljaric describes an increasingly permissive interpretation of international humanitarian law, in which civilian infrastructure is attacked, populations are displaced and human suffering becomes an instrument of military strategy. “So humans are instrumentalized in the pursuit of military objectives,” she observes. The proliferation of drones and artificial intelligence adds another troubling dimension. Technologies once presented as instruments of greater military precision have not, she argues, delivered the promised protection for civilians. Instead, they risk further diminishing the possibility of escaping violence, while the prospect of autonomous weapons targeting human beings raises urgent legal and ethical questions. But Spoljaric's deepest concern extends beyond the battlefield. As conflicts increasingly cross borders and humanitarian needs overwhelm available resources, diplomacy itself appears to be retreating. Her message is ultimately political: humanitarian assistance cannot substitute for the prevention of war, and the protection of civilians cannot depend on goodwill alone. The responsibility, she insists, belongs to governments and citizens alike. “As a citizen, demand that your government prioritize the rules of war,” she urges, warning that “wars are coming to your doorstep nowadays much, much faster than in previous years.”

On Nov. 5, LIFT Airborne Technologies announced it was awarded a 10-year contract with the Air Force for its AV2.2 Next Generation Fixed Wing Helmet system. The contract is worth up to $83.4 million and up to 16,000 helmets, which would be more than enough for all the commissioned fixed-wing aviators in the active-duty Air Force. And Air Force spokesman told Task & Purpose that the service expects deliveries of the helmet to begin in late summer 2027, with the goal of reaching initial operational capability that September. The one fixed-wing community not included in the contract are F-35 fighter pilots, who have their own brain buckets that cost about as much as a Ferrari . All other fixed-wing aviators have worn the HGU-55/P since the 1980s . But times are changing, and the Air Force said it needs different gear to help aircrew stay healthy and to keep up with new technology. That said, it is not clear at this time which units will receive the helmets first. Pain in the neck The HGU-55/P weighs about 2.2 pounds. That may not sound like much, but the pounds add up in high-G maneuvers. A human head weighs about 10 or 11 pounds. That plus a two-pound helmet, plus the weight of any attached heads-up displays or night-vision goggles, and it totals about 120 pounds sitting on the pilot’s neck in a 9G turn. That flexibility should also help as new technology comes online. “From a pre-flight and build-up standpoint, the new helmet is much better,” Airman 1st Class Matthew Crouse, an aircrew flight equipment technician, said in the 2023 release. pending.title: Air Force aims for year-round operations at three Pacific islands
pending.summary: The Air Force intends to use four airfields in the Pacific for more than 6,000 aerial operations per year, as part of its expanding operations in the region. Calling it a “unique opportunity” to support new operational objectives, the Air Force plans to use Saipan International Airport, Tinian International Airport, Tinian North Field and Rota International Airport, all located in the Northern Mariana Islands, for thousands of training flights and aerial exercises per year. The operations are meant to support the service’s Agile Combat Employment, or ACE, strategy, which aims to disperse aerial operations over several locations to avoid creating one large target. The plan was announced in a notice of intent published late in October. The notice calls for getting environmental impact statements on plans to stage aircraft on the three Pacific islands. Here’s why By David Roza According to the notice, the Air Force wants to carry out up to 1,200 fixed-wing and 320 rotary-wing aircraft operations each year per airfield, or more than 6,000 in total annually. To support that, the service would set up temporary infrastructure at each airfield, which would each be staffed by up to 1,000 people. The islands are relatively close to each other and a few dozen miles away from Guam, which has become central to U.S. military planning on potential littoral and island-hopping campaigns in the Pacific. Per the Air Force, the plan would allow it to “test and employ tailorable force packages; exercise movement, sustainment, logistics, and command-and-control functions across multiple locations to replicate the complexity of distributed operations in contingency environments; and strengthen interoperability with Joint, allied, and partner forces within the Mariana Islands region.” There is also an alternative proposal, which could see even more aircraft flights from the four airfields and would allow for “up to 1,400 fixed-wing operations and up to 384 rotary-wing operations per airfield annually.” Draft environmental impact statements are expected next fall. The Air Force has been working to revitalize the airfields at Tinian for the last several years, upgrading infrastructure or in the case of the island’s North Field, clearing “overgrown jungle” to make the installation usable again. The airfields have been used in recent years, as part of multinational exercises like Valiant Shield, but not on the scale proposed here. The Air Force isn’t alone. Other branches have looked to old World War II-era bases in the Pacific as staging grounds for island operations. The Marine Corps has been rehabilitating a historic airfield on Peleliu . Additionally, the overall military has been expanding defenses and bases on Guam , which Air Force documents called “centralized operating installations.” The post Air Force aims for year-round operations at three Pacific islands appeared first on Task & Purpose .

pending.summary: Palestine is becoming a testing ground for artificial intelligence and surveillance technologies that are later exported around the world, a leading Palestinian digital rights advocate has warned, calling for greater accountability for technology companies involved in military operations. In an interview with The New Arab , Nadim Nashif, co-founder and CEO of the Arab Centre for Social Media Advancement (7amleh) , warned that technologies developed or deployed in the occupied Palestinian territories could pose threats far beyond the region. The allegations could not be independently verified, and no publicly available evidence establishes government intervention in specific cases. Speaking after attending the Trust Conference in London on 4 and 5 November, Nashif argued that major technology companies were increasingly moving beyond providing digital services to supplying infrastructure used in military operations. Restrictions on Palestinian content Nashif criticised Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, citing research published by 7amleh in June in collaboration with Fabio Cristiano, a researcher at Utrecht University in the Netherlands. The study examined 3,520 cases reported to the organisation's 7or ("Hurr") monitoring platform for digital violations between 2021 and 2025. According to Nashif, one of its main findings was the repeated use of Meta's Dangerous Organisations and Individuals (DOI) policy to restrict Palestinian content. The policy is intended to address content involving organisations and individuals classified as dangerous, including those associated with terrorism and organised violence. "The company's perspective on Palestinians and pro-Palestinian content is a security-based one, as though this content is suspicious and must be dealt with through deletion or restrictions," Nashif said. The research found that users received no adequate explanation of which policy they had allegedly violated in around 70 percent of documented cases. Meta also failed to respond to almost half of the appeals submitted by 7amleh. Restrictions extended beyond deleting posts and suspending accounts to reducing the reach of content, limiting its appearance in recommendations and restricting livestreaming, measures that users often struggle to identify or challenge. Nashif said Meta employees had described pressure from European governments to impose stricter moderation of pro-Palestinian content, often justified as part of efforts to combat antisemitism. He stressed that antisemitism was a form of racism that must be combated, but warned that such measures became problematic when they restricted legitimate expressions of solidarity with Palestinians or criticism of Israeli policies. In September, 7amleh published a report examining restrictions on pro-Palestinian content in six European countries, including Britain. It documented how platform policies, national legislation and government pressure could affect freedom of expression. pending.summary: No one can mistake me for a supporter of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, or an apologist on his behalf. Over the years, I’ve published hundreds of articles criticizing him and warning of the great damage he has caused to Israel. My criticism only grew stronger after October 7, 2023, when my entire family was almost murdered under his watch. Still, in conversations with American friends who share my dislike for Netanyahu, I often find myself rejecting and correcting one line of criticism: “Netanyahu is just like Trump.” The two populist leaders are close in age and share a similar style of politics, but until recently, they were also separated by a major difference, one that Netanyahu, to my mind, deserved credit for: Unlike Donald Trump, he was not an election denier. When he won—and he did, most of the time—he took the win. But when he lost, he didn’t try to throw out the votes of the Israeli people in order to remain in power. Sadly, this distinction between Trump and Netanyahu no longer holds. Over the past two weeks, Trump has more or less accepted his party’s crushing defeat in the U.S. midterm elections (apart from one social-media post, which I’ll touch on in a moment), while Netanyahu has refused to respect the results of Israel’s election last month and has tried to overturn them in ways that resemble the U.S. president’s role in stoking the events of January 6, 2021. This is something new. When Netanyahu lost reelection in 1999, after his first term as prime minister, he accepted defeat without challenging the foundations of Israeli democracy. He did the same when he led the Likud party to its worst-ever result, in 2006. After his return to power in 2009, he won two more elections, but in 2019 and 2020, he failed three times to win a majority in a series of deadlocked elections. In none of these elections did he try to dispute the results, even though they were uncomfortable for him. The gap that once existed between Netanyahu and Trump was most obvious in 2021. In the first week of that year, Trump’s refusal to accept Joe Biden’s victory, and his cries of a stolen election, paved the way for an armed insurrection. Netanyahu lost power six months later, when Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid succeeded in creating Israel’s short-lived “government of change.” Unlike Trump, he didn’t deny the results or incite his supporters to question the legitimacy of the election. Instead, he moved to the opposition benches of the Knesset and staged a comeback the following year, when the Bennett-Lapid government collapsed. Some fellow Netanyahu critics would point out, correctly, that when Netanyahu lost power in 2021, Biden was in the White House, and therefore any attempt to stage an illegal power grab would have run into strong headwinds from Washington. This is true, but until recently, I believed that even without the threat of a harsh American rebuke, Netanyahu still would have done the right thing and allowed for a peaceful transition of power. The events of the past weeks have convinced me otherwise. On Monday, Trump put up a social-media post in which he questioned for the first time the validity of the midterm results. America mostly shrugged. For now, the president has shown no sign of the dangerous urgency with which he disputed Biden’s victory in 2020. Trump’s original response to the Republican Party’s collapse—he distanced himself from the results (“I wasn’t on the ballot”), blamed specific lawmakers for their losses, and said that the Iran war was worth the electoral shellacking—seems more authentic than his rant about how wrong the polls turned out to be. Israel, however, faces a real crisis that has received relatively little coverage by American media, which has been singularly focused on the midterms. The parties representing the Arab population won only 10 seats out of the Knesset’s total of 120. pending.title: Maldives moves to pass unconditional ban on Israeli tourists
pending.summary: The Maldives is seeking to pass a law that would officially ban Israelis from visiting the island nation on a permanent basis, according to a statement from the office of President Mohamed Muizzu. The announcement of the bill was made at a press conference on Monday. "The current bill provides for an unconditional ban on entry for anyone holding an Israeli passport, irrespective of changing circumstances," the announcement from Muizzu’s office said. The archipelago of about half a million people previously passed legislation banning Israeli passport holders from visiting amid the war on Gaza, where Israeli strikes have continued despite an October 2025 ceasefire. The new bill would tighten these restrictions rather than introduce a first-time ban on Israeli travellers, which came into effect in April 2025. The existing restriction remains in force while the new proposal awaits parliamentary approval. The bill has so far passed its first reading in parliament. According to the president’s statement, the travel ban applies only to people entering on Israeli passports and does not extend to Israelis travelling on a second passport. In December 2023, Israel issued a travel warning advising its citizens against visiting the Maldives, citing rising anti-Israel sentiment during the Gaza war. The Foreign Ministry said Israel could have difficulty assisting them if they encountered trouble there. The Maldives lifted a previous ban on Israeli tourists in the early 1990s and briefly moved to restore relations in 2010. Separately, the Maldivian government has submitted a bill that would bar Israeli citizens and Israeli-owned companies from acquiring leasehold rights in designated development zones. Buyers would be subject to screening, according to local media reports. Unlike the travel ban, these restrictions would also apply to Israelis using a second passport. Muizzu described Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocide , according to the president’s office, and said allowing Israeli passport holders into the country was unacceptable. Both bills still require parliamentary approval. The Maldives, a small country comprising 1,192 strategically located coral islands, is known for its secluded white-sand beaches, shallow turquoise lagoons and Robinson Crusoe-style getaways. Its population is nearly all Muslim.

pending.summary: Does Donald Trump mean anything? The question could be asked about the president’s promises, which he usually fails to keep, and his podium remarks, which are devoted to free association. But for conservative politicians, policy makers, and intellectuals, the question has a wider bearing. Since 2016, the right has been trying to figure out what Trump means as a political phenomenon. Presidents are transformative when they stand for an idea: Ronald Reagan was personally popular, but what made him historic was the reorientation of American politics toward Reaganism, an assertive brand of small-government, big-stick conservatism. Trump has certainly been transformative, so it stands to reason that there is such a thing as Trumpism. Like pornography, we feel that we know Trumpism when we see it, yet after a decade, it’s still remarkably hard to define. That blurriness has been an opportunity for political entrepreneurs who have tried, one after another, to shape Trumpism in the image of their own ideological beliefs. pending.title: Palestinian journalists faced 134 Israeli violations in October
pending.summary: Israeli forces and settlers were responsible for at least 134 reported violations against Palestinian journalists and media institutions last month, with the occupied West Bank city of Hebron the worst-affected area, according to a new report published on Thursday. The Palestinian Journalists Syndicate’s Freedoms Committee's report details 134 crimes, attacks and violations against Palestinian journalists and media institutions in October 2026. The incidents were mostly committed by Israeli forces and settlers but also involve Israeli military courts. According to the committee’s monthly report, the violations included measures intended to obstruct journalists' work and restrict their ability to cover events. These included detentions, reporting bans, arrests, harassment, threats and raids on journalists’ homes and media institutions. Detentions and restrictions on media coverage accounted for the largest number of incidents, with 70 cases, followed by 27 incidents involving tear gas and stun grenades. The report also documented eight raids on journalists’ homes and media institutions, seven arrests and an equal number of cases in which journalists were referred to military courts. The report also highlighted physical attacks against Palestinian journalists, documenting three cases of journalists being wounded by live ammunition, one of whom was also injured by missile shrapnel. It further recorded five attacks by Israeli settlers. In addition, three journalists were subjected to questioning, while two cases involved threats and incitement. One journalist was also handed a financial fine. Hebron recorded the highest number of violations, particularly detentions of media crews, restrictions on coverage and the use of tear gas and stun grenades against journalists. These incidents took plac e amid an 11-day Israeli siege on the city , which resulted in the mass displacement of Palestinians. Last Tuesday, Al Jazeera reported that its correspondent Montaser Nasser had been arrested during an Israeli raid on his home in Dura, near Hebron. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) reported last month that Israeli forces had also detained reporters, fired tear gas and directed lasers at news crews during a major raid in Hebron, describing the incidents as part of “escalating violence” against the media. CPJ added that these incidents followed a series of violations by Israeli soldiers and settlers targeting Palestinian and international journalists in the occupied West Bank, particularly while they were covering the ongoing olive harvest , which has seen a series of attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinian farmers. The International Federation of Journalists (IFJ) reported that at least five journalists and media workers had been arrested by Israeli forces or attacked by Israeli settlers while covering the olive harvest in the occupied West Bank since October. It said the incidents reflected a wider pattern of violence, intimidation and repression targeting local and international journalists reporting in Palestine. Since the beginning of Israel's genocidal war on Gaza on 7 October 2023 , Israeli military violence against journalists has escalated, with 24 times as many journalists killed and three times as many detained, according to Reporters Without Borders (RSF). RSF has described Israel as one of the world's ten largest prisons for journalists for the fourth consecutive year.

ready.title: 3 Iranian-backed men indicted in attempted plot on RAF Fairford
ready.summary: Federal prosecutors allege that an Iranian terrorist proxy group’s commander, alongside two other men, assisted in orchestrating the suspected terror plot on a United Kingdom military base from jail while awaiting trial on other pending terrorism charges. From jail in New York, Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national, allegedly coordinated with Mohammad Ali al-Hassani and Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iraqi and Iranian national, respectively, to organize the recent failed terror attack on RAF Fairford , according to a recent Department of Justice release . The three men allegedly conspired to commit nearly 20 terrorist attacks and attempted attacks across Europe and the U.S. in the name of two Iran-aligned terrorist networks that are designated by the U.S. as Foreign Terrorist Organizations, per an eight-count indictment. “Even after one of their co-conspirators was arrested and placed in federal custody, the defendants allegedly continued coordinating terrorist activity through coded communications and a network of associates overseas,” U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald for the Southern District of New York said in the release. “The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real.” The indictment says that most recently, al-Hassani, with terrorism-related offenses for their activities in support of Kataib Hezbollah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, allegedly managed the September plot on RAF Fairford, which housed U.S. military aircraft and personnel at the time in support of the war in Iran. In the Southern District of New York, al-Saadi was in jail awaiting trial on pending terrorism charges and tried to correspond with al-Hassani and Mohajeri by passing coded messages through third parties. Al-Hassani and Mohajeri were both in Iran at the time of the attempted RAF Fairford scheme, so they relied on a network of contacts in the U.K., per the statement. Al-Saadi was charged in May for collaborating with and working on behalf of the IRGC, other FTOs and Kataib Hezbollah, an Iraqi militia group that he is the commander of and that is backed by the IRGC. He was also charged for his participation in planning and promoting around 18 terrorist attacks in Europe and for attempting to bomb a synagogue in New York. The indictment alleges that al-Hassani and Mohajeri, an operative of the IRGC, worked with al-Saadi to facilitate and complete many of the European terrorist attacks. Al-Hassani used his contacts and criminal associates to carry out attacks in the U.K., prosecutors allege. Al-Saadi was arrested abroad in early May and transferred to U.S. custody for prosecution, staying in federal custody since his arrival in the U.S. For four months following his arrest, there were no additional attacks attributed to the three men. Then in August, prosecutors say that al-Hassani directed and paid associates in the U.K. to conduct “preparatory steps” for the RAF Fairford plot, such as surveillance of the base’s perimeter. The next month, he also paid several people to assist in the plot’s preparation, like procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching chemical accelerants and purchasing items that could be used as explosive shrapnel. In late September, al-Hassani supposedly told individuals to drive three vans, some with barrels of fuel inside, to RAF Fairford, but at least two encountered a security roadblock and were not able to continue to the base. U.K. law enforcement authorities later recovered three white vans and arrested the individuals. While in jail, al-Saadi allegedly used phone calls with his family in Iraq to pass coded messages to al-Hassani and Mohajeri in the days leading up to the RAF Fairford plot. Three days before the attempted plot, al-Saadi spoke with his family on the phone and inquired about how al-Hassani was doing, telling them to give him money so “we can do it.” The eight-count indictment lists six charges for all three with a total maximum penalty of 90 years in prison or life in prison, and two charges reserved only for al-Saadi, with a maximum of 20 years or life in prison.

previous_post.fa_title: کشته شدن فرمانده تیپ خان‌یونس حماس در حمله اسرائیل به بیمارستان ناصر
paras: ارتش اسرائیل با تایید حمله هوایی به بیمارستان ناصر در خان‌یونس، اعلام کرد که در این عملیات «محمد ابواسماعیل»، فرمانده تیپ خان‌یونس حماس را هدف قرار داده است. این حمله که به گفته مقامات بهداشتی غزه مرگبارترین عملیات از زمان انتخابات اخیر اسرائیل بوده، منجر به کشته شدن ۶ نفر و مجروح شدن نزدیک به ۳۰ تن شده است.

شاهدان عینی و کادر درمان گزارش دادند که بخش جراحی این بیمارستان بدون هشدار قبلی هدف بمب‌های جنگنده‌های اف-۱۶ قرار گرفته و تجهیزات پزشکی و ساختمان دچار خسارات جدی شده است. حماس با رد ادعای اسرائیل مبنی بر استفاده نظامی از این مرکز درمانی، این اقدام را جنایت جنگی خواند.

این حمله در حالی صورت گرفت که اسرائیل و حماس همچنان یکدیگر را به نقض توافق آتش‌بس تحت حمایت آمریکا متهم می‌کنند. طبق گزارش‌ها، در جریان این حادثه، یک نفر دیگر نیز بر اثر تیراندازی نیروهای اسرائیلی در اردوگاه البریج کشته شده است که ارتش اسرائیل اعلام کرده در حال بررسی آن است.

ready.title: Saudi Arabia puts pressure on EU to label Yemen's Houthis a terrorist group
ready.summary: By Alexander Cornwell Nov 12 (Reuters) - Saudi Arabia is pressing the EU to designate Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi movement as a terrorist organisation, but has yet to overcome European concerns that this could undermine a future peace process, according to six European officials. The campaign reflects a broader effort by Riyadh to increase international pressure on the group, which has been carrying out near-daily attacks on the kingdom in recent weeks after the resumption of war that began more than a decade ago.
ready.fa_title: فشار ریاض بر اتحادیه اروپا برای قرار دادن انصارالله یمن در فهرست تروریسم
paras: عربستان سعودی در راستای تشدید فشارهای بین‌المللی بر انصارالله یمن، در حال رایزنی با اتحادیه اروپا است تا این جنبش را به عنوان یک سازمان تروریستی معرفی کند؛ با این حال دیپلمات‌های اروپایی هشدار داده‌اند که این تصمیم نیازمند اجماع هر ۲۷ عضو است و تاکنون تنها کشورهای اندکی از آن حمایت کرده‌اند.

نگرانی اصلی پایتخت‌های اروپایی این است که تروریستی نامیدن انصارالله یمن، مسیرهای ارتباطی محدود برای مذاکرات صلح آینده را مسدود کند و علاوه بر پیچیده‌تر کردن ارسال کمک‌های بشردوستانه، خطر پاسخ تلافی‌جویانه و هدف قرار گرفتن کشتی‌های اروپایی در دریای سرخ و تنگه باب‌المندب را افزایش دهد.

پیش از این پارلمان اروپا طی قطعنامه‌ای نمادین خواستار این اقدام شده بود، اما لغو احتمالی چنین برچسبی طبق قوانین اتحادیه نیازمند اجماع کامل اعضا خواهد بود. هم‌اکنون برخی از رهبران انصارالله و محموله‌های تسلیحاتی تحت تحریم‌های اروپا قرار دارند و سپاه پاسداران ایران نیز توسط این اتحادیه تروریستی اعلام شده است.

ready.title: Germany, Poland tap SATIM to analyze military satellite imagery
ready.summary: WARSAW, Poland — SATIM, a Polish maker of AI-based analysis tools for synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery, has obtained a contract from Poland’s Ministry of National Defence to supply software for the automated analysis of satellite imagery. The company is building on its ongoing cooperation with Germany’s Rheinmetall to support the German SPOCK-1 satellite reconnaissance program. The solution will support Warsaw’s MikroSAR earth-observation program, SATIM said in a Nov. 12 statement. Advanced by a consortium of Finland’s ICEYE and Wojskowe Zakłady Łączności No 1, a subsidiary of Polish state-run defense group PGZ, the national satellite reconnaissance system is the first component of the military space capabilities Poland aims to develop in the coming years. “Access to SAR imagery is only the first step. The value comes from extracting useful intelligence quickly, consistently and at scale,” said Jacek Strzelczyk, the CEO of SATIM. “This contract allows us to support Poland’s sovereign reconnaissance capabilities and demonstrate how automated analysis helps analysts make more effective use of radar data.” SAR satellites can acquire imagery regardless of sunlight conditions and through cloud cover. However, interpreting the collected imagery and properly identifying detected military equipment can be both a challenging and time-consuming process. These difficulties create opportunities for specialized software suppliers such as SATIM, according to company representatives. “Interest among users increased following the outbreak of the war in Ukraine where cloud cover is frequently an issue. SAR radars can see through clouds, but their imagery is also very difficult to interpret. Our solution offers a very high level of accuracy, reaching 90–95% for most object classes,” Mateusz Raczyński, a SATIM spokesperson, told Defense News. “We can identify objects across approximately 300 classes, including vessels, aircraft, and vehicles.” On Nov. 2, SATIM announced that it had reached another milestone with Rheinmetall in their collaboration supporting the SPOCK-1 program. “The automated analysis pipeline supplied by SATIM to Rheinmetall has now entered operational testing phase, supporting the German Armed Forces’ analysis of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery,” the Polish business said. Meanwhile, SATIM is working on securing further customers for its services across the world. “Being a Polish company, we first established cooperation with the German industry that was open to validating our software and after that including it to support the SPOCK-1 program, one of the major ISR programs globally. Now we are also extending our work with Poland,” Raczyński said. “We are also active in other markets. Our solutions are used in the United States, Japan, Qatar, and the UAE. Next month, we are going to Vietnam to explore this market, as well.”
ready.fa_title: توسعه سامانه هوش مصنوعی برای تحلیل تصاویر راداری ماهواره‌ای در لهستان و آلمان
paras: شرکت لهستانی ساتیِم (SATIM)، سازنده ابزارهای تحلیلی مبتنی بر هوش مصنوعی برای تصاویر راداری دهانه ترکیبی (SAR)، قراردادی را با وزارت دفاع ملی لهستان برای تأمین نرم‌افزار تحلیل خودکار تصاویر ماهواره‌ای منعقد کرد. این پروژه بخشی از برنامه ملی دیده‌بانی زمین MikroSAR برای توسعه توانمندی‌های فضایی نظامی این کشور است.

این شرکت همزمان همکاری‌های خود را با راین‌متال آلمان در چارچوب برنامه شناسایی ماهواره‌ای SPOCK-1 توسعه داده است. به گفته این شرکت، فناوری تحلیل خودکار راداری وارد فاز آزمایش عملیاتی برای ارتش آلمان شده و ابزار موثری جهت پایش اهداف نظامی به شمار می‌رود.

رادارهای سار بر خلاف تجهیزات نوری توانایی رصد اهداف از میان ابرها و در تاریکی شب را دارند، اما تفسیر داده‌های آن‌ها پیچیده است. به گفته سخنگوی ساتیِم، این الگوریتم‌ها با دقت ۹۰ تا ۹۵ درصد می‌توانند نزدیک به ۳۰۰ رده تجهیزات نظامی شامل شناورها، بالگردها و خودروها را شناسایی کنند.

ready.title: BREAKING: USS South Dakota Command Triad Relieved After October Grounding, Congressman Says
ready.summary: 11-gun salutes are fired for the arrival of Rear Adm. Melvin Smith, Commander, Submarine Group 2, during the Virginia-class nuclear-powered fast attack submarine USS South Dakota (SSN-790) Change of Command Ceremony at Naval Submarine Base New London in Groton, Connecticut, June 30, 2026. Cmdr. Daniel Goodwin relieved Cmdr. Burnes C.W. Brown as Commanding Officer of South Dakota. US Navy photo USS South Dakota (SSN-790) command triad was removed last month following a grounding incident, according to a statement from a member of Congress. The submarine’s commanding officer, executive officer and chief of the boat were relieved from command on Oct. 14, with the relief allegedly attributed to a grounding incident, according to a letter released Thursday by Reps. Joe Courtney (D-Conn.), Ranking Member of the House Seapower and Projection Forces Subcommittee, and Adam Smith (D-Wash.), Ranking Member of the House Armed Services Committee. Cmdr. Dan Goodwin was relieved as commander of South Dakota , according to a story in the Day newspaper based in New London, Conn. Goodwin assumed command of South Dakota in June of 2026, according to a Pentagon release . Lawmakers learned of the relief from a reporter’s request for comment on the dismissal, according to the letter. Nearly one month later, no notifications of the firings or the underlying incident had been made to the House Armed Services Committee. Cmdr. Daniel Goodwin, commanding officer of USS South Dakota (SSN-790) is piped ashore following the USS South Dakota (SSN-790) change of command ceremony that was held June 30, 2026, onboard the fast attack submarine pierside at Naval Submarine Base New London in Groton, Conn. US Navy photo “The Department of the Navy’s failure to communicate these incidents to Congress is unacceptable,” reads the letter, which is addressed to Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao and Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle. The Navy typically informs Congress of at-sea incidents, accidents and dismissals of command triads. “The Navy’s lack of transparency leave many outstanding questions about not only what occurred, but the impact of the events leading the triad’s dismissal on the structural health of South Dakota , the well-being of the crew, and whether the incident laid bare any systemic issues with training to standard procedures that must be addressed. As a result of the Navy’s failure to communicate, what should have been a standard exercise in information sharing has instead raised questions about the Navy’s commitment to transparency and its commitment to a productive working relationship with Congress,” reads the letter. A defense official confirmed the removals to USNI News. A Navy spokesperson acknowledged a question from USNI News but did not immediately provide a comment. USNI News editor Sam LaGrone contributed to this report.

ready.title: Nine-month-old baby dies of cold in Gaza
ready.summary: A nine-month-old baby died of hypothermia on Thursday, his father and a doctor told AFP , after days of harsh weather and flooding in the Gaza Strip that displaced thousands of Palestinians living in tents. The doctor, who saw the child and spoke on condition of anonymity, said that nine-month-old Kinan Ahmed Raqiq "died from hypothermia inside his family's displacement tent" in Khan Younis, in the southern Gaza Strip. Ahmed Raqiq, told AFP that his son Kinan died of cold during the night in their tent in southern Gaza. "I woke up only to see his skin had turned blue so I rushed him to Nasser hospital , but he had already died from hypothermia and frozen to death," he said. "I am in complete shock. I found myself holding my son wrapped in burial shroud," he said outside the hospital, dried tears on his face as he held his son wrapped in a white sheet. Heavy rain last week flooded tens of thousands of people's tents in Gaza, where virtually the whole population has been displaced at least once by three years of Israeli strikes in response to the 7 October 2023 attack by Hamas. Five people including three children died the day after the flooding when a sandy embankment collapsed onto their tents. Rain and cold Since then, hundreds of displaced families have been seen fleeing camps in parts of Gaza City and central and northern areas of the territory after they were inundated by rainwater. James Elder, spokesman on Gaza for the UN children's agency, UNICEF, warned that the flooding was just the beginning of the cold season. "It's very important to know how bad things are in Gaza. It's not yet winter," Elder said. "We're weeks away from winter, so we are getting unprecedented rain and cold." The UN's Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said that as of November 8, 26,000 households were affected by storms. Around 65% of Gaza's people are still living displaced in tents or other temporary shelter, OCHA said. Israel and Hamas declared a ceasefire on October 10, 2025 but Israel has kept striking the territory, vowing to kill anyone involved in the 7 October attack, the deadliest in Israel's history. In rare criticism, President Donald Trump's Board of Peace said this week that Israel - which tightly controls entry into Gaza - had not done enough in anticipation of the cold weather and that it needed urgently to let in more supplies. Caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in a response to the Board of Peace, said that Israel had allowed in supplies including 91,000 tents and that "Hamas alone is responsible for the suffering of the people of Gaza". "Hamas must not be allowed to exploit humanitarian supplies and equipment to rebuild its terror capabilities," Netanyahu said. (AFP)
